1284.dq: Word-stress in KM is phonemic. In the vast majority of words it is on the penult.
1284.dloc: Steinhauer 1983: 44, section 2.2 (Phonology); Paauw 2009: 454-455 (A.5.3.2 Vowels of Kupang Malay, ex. A448)
1284.heavy: A penult containing /ə/ or /A/ rejects stress, which then 'always falls on the final syllable (unless this contains /ə/, in which case it is on the penult again)' — e.g. [kə'na] 'to be struck' but /'səstər/ 'nurse'; the other vowels /i e a o u/ count as full.
1284.prule: Word stress is phonemic (lexically contrastive) within the last two syllables: default penultimate ('vast majority of words'); obligatorily final when the penult contains /ə/ or /A/ (unless the final syllable also has /ə/); and an unpredictable lexical set of words with final stress despite a full penult vowel (minimal pairs 'barat 'west' vs ba'rat 'heavy', 'batu vs ba'tu, 'parut vs pa'rut, etc.; historically from Vehicular Malay schwa penults, Paauw 2009).
1284.srule: Not mentioned in Steinhauer 1983, sec. 2.0-2.3 Phonology, pp. 44-45 (word stress: sec. 2.2, p. 44); likewise not mentioned in Paauw 2009: 453-454 or Culhane & Kaland 2025.

1285.dq: In words which have only two syllables the accent is always on the first: puddā, short; bāckā, word.
1285.dloc: Chapter II, C. Accentuation, sec. 13, p. 9 (archive.org leaf n26)
1285.prule: Accent position depends on word class: disyllables always initial; trisyllabic verbs (infinitive citation forms in -nā) generally on the 2nd syllable, those ending in -ba'anā on the 3rd, rare verbs initial (nisigna, nedegnā); adverbs initial even at 3-4 syllables, except compounds, which accent the first syllable of the second member; nouns of 3-4 syllables mostly initial, seldom 2nd (barandō), very rarely 3rd (durbehār). No single quantity-insensitive position; no weight criterion stated.
1285.srule: Not mentioned in Hahn 1911 (Ch. II C 'Accentuation', sec. 13, p. 9 = the whole accent section; sec. 8, pp. 6-7, also read): Hahn assigns one 'accent' per word, including four-syllable nouns and adverbs, and says nothing about secondary or rhythmic stress.

1286.dq: A sílaba tônica é invariavelmente a última do vocábulo ... Na formação de radicais, quando palavras acentuadas encontram-se, mantém-se apenas o acento do último vocábulo. O mesmo acontece quando o último morfema é um sufixo
1286.prule: Word stress is non-contrastive and falls invariably on the last syllable of the word (Costa 2002:97 = Costa 1998:36; endorsed from her own fieldwork by Silva 2009:46 'Esse fato parece ser verdadeiro'); quantity-insensitive, no conditioning stated. In stem/compound formation and under suffixation only the stress of the last word/morpheme is kept, i.e. stress is final over the whole morphological word.
1286.srule: None: one stress per word -- 'A sílaba tônica é invariavelmente a última do vocábulo... quando palavras acentuadas encontram-se, mantém-se apenas o acento do último vocábulo. O mesmo acontece quando o último morfema é um sufixo' (non-final members of compounds and suffixed stems lose their stress; seven-syllable [darakudʲi£ubi*a] carries a single stress mark). No secondary or rhythmic stress is described anywhere in the article; Mendes 2007:49 and Silva 2009:46 likewise mention only the final stress.
1286.quote: Quanto ao acento, este não é contrastivo. A sílaba tônica é invariavelmente a última do vocábulo, por essa razão, não há necessidade de marcá-la na transcrição fonológica: (48) a. [para*wa] /parawa/ ‘arara’ b. [parawa*tô] /parawatô/ ‘arara azul’ c. [daraku*dʲi] /darakodʲi/ ‘galinha’ d. [tubi*a] /tobia/ ‘ovo’ Na formação de radicais, quando palavras acentuadas encontram-se, mantém-se apenas o acento do último vocábulo. O mesmo acontece quando o último morfema é um sufixo: (49) a. [daraku*dʲi] ‘galinha’ + [tubi*a] ‘ovo’ > [darakudʲi£ubi*a] /darakodʲi£obia/ ‘ovo de galinha’ ...

1286.tone: The primary asserts (tentative) lexical tone ALONGSIDE fixed final stress. Costa 2002:98-99, sec. 6 'O tom': 'Pode-se dizer que o Kuruaya é uma língua tonal, fato que se demonstra pelos seguintes aspectos: i. Há uma configuração tonal recorrente evidenciada pela presença de dois tons: alto e baixo (aqui representados respectivamente por ¹ e ²). Todos os padrões silábicos podem ocorrer com qualquer um dos tons, tanto em sílaba tônica quanto em átona.... ii. Além disso, dois pares mínimos tonais foram encontrados:... Embora até o momento haja somente esses pares que comprovam a distinção do significado a partir do tom, este não deve ser desconsiderado'. Conclusion p. 100: 'todos os indícios levam a crer tratar-se de uma língua tonal, cujo sistema tonológico é composto... por dois tons: alto e baixo.' Stress is treated separately (p. 97) as non-contrastive and invariably word-final, with tone free with respect to the tonic syllable, so in Costa's description a two-level tone contrast (hedged; 2 minimal pairs) and fixed final stress coexist. Silva 2009 defers 'acento e tom' to future research; sister language Mundurukú is tonal (Picanço 2005). Under our rule 8 tone or pitch accent is reserved for tone systems with no stress rule, so fixed and quantity-insensitive stands, but downstream users excluding tone languages must see this flag.

1287.prule: Stress is a property of roots: every root (roots are monosyllabic, (C)VV or (C)V(V)C) carries underlying stress, so the stressed syllable is the root syllable = stem-initial (word-initial in unprefixed words; on the post-prefix root syllable in prefixed nominals, e.g. pʋ̄kɔ̀ɔⁿr stressed on -kɔ̀ɔⁿr). Stress co-exists with a four-tone lexical tone system (H M L X, syllable = TBU) and conditions tone realisation (MH -> MM+downstep before a stressed syllable).

1288.prule: No stress rule is stated for the language. The only statement is a transcription convention for the 1894 wordlist: unmarked entries are stressed on the penult; entries whose stress deviates carry a written acute. On the one list page checked in image (p. 530, ~100 entries) about two thirds are unmarked (penult by convention) and roughly a quarter to a third carry a marked accent, mostly word-final (papá, atú, atší, uá, itsá, piuá, amaká, palatá, zapalakú, yaká, nukayá, uhú, höká, hemirzá, kisuá, pauá, taputá, kumá, aitzá), a few on a final vowel sequence (numái, nutái, nukái, kulupéi, uléi) and a few antepenult (papáluka, nukitsíui). Penult is thus the majority position but final stress is common and item-specific; the source gives no conditioning.

1295.prule: Word stress is largely predictable but morphologically governed: monomorphemic lexical words (and proper names) take final stress; in polymorphemic words a closed set of suffixes (definite -a/-ka, plural -al, comparative/superlative -tir/-tirīn, 'another' tir, ordinal -im/-om) attract primary stress (last such host wins), while another set (indefinite -e/-ī(k), indicative =a, demonstrative =a, cliticized prepositions, bound pronouns, enclitic copula, additive =īš, conjunction =ö, ezafe =i, compounding =a) are unstressed and follow the stress; in verbs ('a higher degree of variability'), Infinitives are final-stressed, indicative ma- and subjunctive bi- are as a rule unstressed (stress on ending or root), indicative negative ni- usually attracts stress, subjunctive negative na- does not, but bi- and na- may carry stress in Imperatives (bíka!, náka!); Preterite stresses the stem, Perfect the syllable before the present clitic copula, Pluperfect the past clitic copula; hence stress is distinctive across morphological categories (kirdín 'to do' vs kírdin 'they did').

1300.dq: A phonological word consists of an obligatory nucleus plus optional onset and final peripheries. ... The nucleus is filled by a syllable which has an inherent toneme; the tones of the syllables which fill the peripheries depend on the tone which is on the nucleus of the word

1300.prule: No stress rule stated anywhere in the phonology. Vowel length, prenasalization and labialization are likewise features of the nuclear syllable only.

1300.tone: Grebe & Grebe 1976 never use the words stress, accent or prominence (full-text search of all 54 pp: zero hits). The phonological word has a nucleus/periphery structure: one obligatory nuclear syllable (the monosyllabic root) carries the full 8-way tone contrast, vowel length, prenasalization and labialization; peripheral (affixal) syllables are CV/N with predictable L or low-falling tone and never long. This is a root-culminative tonal system, not a stress system; Grebe 1984 (MA thesis) likewise treats noun prosody purely as lexical/floating tone ('Lam Nso noun roots are monosyllabic').

There is more affixation in the nominal domain: inflectional affixes include possessor-indexing suffixes marking inalienable possession, the prefix na- 'ART' encoding genericity, and the nominaliser suffix –na 'NMLZ'." 1308.quote: A phonological word in Lele can be defined using the following criteria: 1. The phonological word cannot be interrupted 2. There is one main accent assigned to each phonological word 3. morph.stmt: Lenje is a typically Bantu prefixing-and-suffixing language with inflection predominantly prefixal and derivation suffixal: 'In general, these distinctions are marked by prefixes, syllables placed before the root, and affixes placed after it, in a certain order, viz. prefixes of person first, then those of tense, then the root, with affixes showing stem and voice. tn.quote: Tone is marked on the tone carrier unit. There is a high level tone (described as 7, v is a tone carrier unit), a low level tone (V, no mark) and an ultra-low level tone (¥). Furthermore, there is a falling tone from high, a falling tone from low (V) and a falling tone from ultra-low (V). The ultra-low level tone and these falling tones appear only at the sentence-final position. The tone in parentheses is optional. A sequence of consecutive tones is called a tonal pattern. wee is called the tonal slippage mark in this study, and it lowers all tones by one level after the mark.

morph.stmt: Predominantly suffixing plus proclitic: 'Central Lembata has a head-marking structure which is manifested in bound pronouns that mark arguments on the verb... there is one proclitic set, one prefix set and two suffix sets' (§3.4.2.5 p.97); 'Nouns in Central Lembata have only one slot for suffixes' (possessor / -u spec / -ja pl; §3.3.1 p.51); 'For words with more than two syllables, the last syllable is usually a suffix' (§3.2.4 p.48); the only true prefixes are single-consonant S/A person prefixes on ~16 vowel-initial verb roots, and derivational prefix/infix morphology (nominalising -n-/b-, verbalising g-) 'appear[s] to be fossilised nowadays' (§3.3.6 p.79, §3.5.4 p.111).
